title: Control Plane TLS Inspection Mitigation Playbook
body:
Summary:

Working playbook + incident review notes for recurring short-duration control-plane reachability degradations we've observed with customers behind enterprise customer-side TLS inspection (transparent TLS proxies / enterprise NGFWs with TLS interception). This doc captures observed signal, mitigation steps we can recommend to customers, quick triage commands for on-call, and a short analysis of root cause hypotheses.

Why this matters:
- Symptoms: rapid connection resets or 502/504s from control-plane endpoints (API control, config sync, health checks) that correlate with bursts of TLS re-negotiation from customer edge devices.
- Impact: customer agents lose control-plane heartbeat for ~15-90s, autoscaler or config changes get delayed, private deployment control plane reconnect flaps. Intermittent but high-severity for some customers.

Observed signals (recent incidents):
- Elevated TLS handshake failures in control-plane logs (tls: handshake error: EOF) between 2026-02-18 and 2026-02-24.
- TCP RST bursts on port 443 from customer NAT blocks visible in netflow export.
- Customer FW telemetries shows active TLS inspection proxy issuing new self-signed certs for each session, causing frequent session renegotiation and short-lived TLS session resumption failures.
- On our side, KV cache re-inits and RPC backoff spikes matching the periods.

Quick triage checklist (on-call):
1) Confirm alert correlation: check control-plane svc logs (last 30m) and look for handshake errors + peer IPs.
   - command: sudo journalctl -u controlplane -n 500 | grep -i "handshake"
2) Check connection-level stats: tcpdump capture (5m) on control plane frontend to confirm multiple ClientHello sequences from same client IPs.
   - command: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host <customer-ip> and port 443 -w /tmp/tls-inspect.pcap
3) Check proxy/edge metrics: look at request latency histogram and open connections. If we see spikes in SSL renegotiation counts, note them.
4) Contact customer SRE/account lead: ask whether they have TLS inspection enabled and whether recent policy changes were applied. Frame as: "We see repeated TLS re-handshakes from your edge—any recent NGFW changes?"

Mitigation options (ordered quick->persistent):
A) Short-term (on-call): request customer to whitelist Redwood control-plane IPs/hostnames from TLS inspection for the control-plane-control traffic. This often eliminates renegotiation loops immediately.
B) Medium-term: suggest configuring the customer's TLS inspection device to allow TLS passthrough or to preserve session resumption (enable TLS session tickets/resumption). Provide example config snippets for common vendors (Palo Alto, F5, Fortinet) in Confluence link.
C) Persistent: for customers who can't disable inspection, run on-prem side keepalive / connection pinning tweaks: increase keepalive, extend TLS session timeout client-side, and enable persistent HTTP/2 connections where possible. Note: changes require coordination with the infra team and customer.

Proposed runbook steps to implement (draft):
- Preconditions: need control-plane logs access and customer point-of-contact.
- Step 1: Enable debug TLS logging for 1 hour to capture handshake sequences and certificate chains. (rotate logs after capture).
- Step 2: Capture packet trace for 10 minutes around the incident window. Upload to secure bucket and share with customer for cross-correlation.
- Step 3: If TLS inspection is confirmed, recommend immediate whitelist of these FQDNs/IPs: controlplane.redwood.internal, cp-sync.redwood.internal (fill with customer-facing hostnames as appropriate).
- Step 4: If whitelist not possible, apply temporary connection policy on the control-plane ingress layer: bump max TLS session timeout to 24h, increase idle keepalive to 120s, and reduce aggressive connection churn settings. (Requires infra-ops change request).
- Step 5: Post-mitigation: monitor for 24h, collect RTT and handshake error rates, and schedule follow-up call.

Root cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) Customer TLS interceptors terminate TLS and re-originate sessions without supporting session resumption or ticketing correctly. Each proxied session gets new certs and causes client-server state mismatches.
2) Middlebox / enterprise NGFWs are aggressively killing idle TLS sessions as part of security posture updates (e.g., after IPS signature updates), leading to bursty reconnections.
3) NAT translation limits + ephemeral port exhaustion on customer side causing RSTs seen as TLS failures.

Evidence mapping: we saw repeated ClientHello from same source IPs (hypothesis 1), and customers reported recent NGFW rule pushes (hypothesis 2) in two incidents. Port exhaustion was present in one case but didn't match TLS error patterns (hypothesis 3 lower confidence).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Can we instrument our ephemeral connection reuse more aggressively in the agent to survive TLS interceptions? (action: product + infra spike, ticket INFRA-1034)
- Add a non-TLS control-plane heartbeat option behind VPC peering for customers who require deep TLS inspection? (action: security review)
- Collect structured metrics for TLS re-negotiation counts per customer to trigger automated mitigation. (action: observability team, ticket OBS-221)

Customer communication template (on-call copy/paste):
"Hi <customer-sre>, we observed repeated TLS re-handshakes between our control-plane endpoint and your edge devices around <time>. This often indicates an active TLS inspection or proxy that terminates+re-initiates TLS sessions. Can you confirm whether TLS inspection was recently enabled or updated? Quick test that often resolves this is to whitelist our control-plane FQDNs from interception for control-plane traffic. If whitelisting isn't possible, we can coordinate a configuration change window to adjust timeouts.

If helpful, we can run an on-call debug capture and share the pcap over the secure channel. Let us know a preferred point of contact and a time window of 30–60 minutes."

Post-incident notes (recent run):
- 2026-02-20 incident with AcmeCorp: whitelist request resolved connectivity in 9 minutes, no further flaps.
- 2026-02-22 incident with NovaBank: required vendor change (Fortinet session ticket preserve setting) and a short agent keepalive tweak; resolution within 6 hours.

Next steps (owners assigned):
- Evan Park: formalize Confluence vendor snippets and add to playbook. (due 2026-03-31)
- Aisha Kapoor: OBS ticket to add TLS renegotiation counter in control-plane metrics. (due 2026-04-07)
- Miguel Santos: infra change proposal for safe TLS session timeout bump and necessary rollout plan. (due 2026-03-20)

Notes to self: keep this doc lightweight and action oriented; customers prefer quick whitelist > long config guidance. Add sample CLI commands for common vendor GUIs.

Appendix (links and quick commands):
- tcpdump example: sudo tcpdump -i any host <customer-ip> and port 443 -w /tmp/cp-inspect.pcap
- journal query example: sudo journalctl -u controlplane --since "30 minutes ago" | grep -i "tls\|handshake\|reset"
- Related tickets: JIRA-PI-4521 (AcmeCorp incident), JIRA-OPS-490 (NovaBank vendor fix)
